claim: The vertebrate skull varies widely in shape, accommodating diverse strategies of feeding and predation.
source: The vertebrate skull varies widely in shape, accommodating diverse strategies of feeding and predation.
evidence: This is a general statement about vertebrate skull diversity, drawing from established scientific knowledge about vertebrate morphology and ecology.

claim: The braincase is composed of several flat bones that meet at flexible joints called sutures.
source: The braincase is composed of several flat bones that meet at flexible joints called sutures.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about vertebrate skull structure.

claim: Nearly all vertebrates have a prominent 'coronal' suture that separates the front and back of the skull.
source: Nearly all vertebrates have a prominent 'coronal' suture that separates the front and back of the skull.
evidence: This is a general anatomical observation about vertebrate skull structure.

claim: The coronal suture can develop entirely within mesoderm-derived tissue, neural crest-derived tissue, or at the boundary of the two.
source: This suture can develop entirely within mesoderm-derived tissue, neural crest-derived tissue, or at the boundary of the two.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing studies discussed later in the manuscript.

claim: Embryonic calvarial bones grow through addition of new osteoblasts at their leading edges.
source: Embryonic calvarial bones then grow through addition of new osteoblasts at their leading edges, until bone covers the majority of the roof of the head.
evidence: This describes a known developmental process of calvarial bone growth.

claim: Sutures serve as flexible attachment sites between bones and house progenitor cells that allow further growth of the bones and hence growth of the skull and brain.
source: These sutures serve as flexible attachment sites between bones, and house progenitor cells that allow further growth of the bones and hence growth of the skull and brain (Doro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doro et al., 2017.

claim: Sutures provide a source of osteoblasts for bone repair.
source: Sutures also provide a source of osteoblasts for bone repair (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: Major sutures in humans include the coronal (interface of frontal and parietal bones), sagittal (parietal-parietal), metopic (frontal-frontal), and lambdoid (parietal-supraoccipital).
source: As defined for humans, major sutures include the coronal (interface of frontal and parietal bones), sagittal (parietal-parietal), metopic (frontal-frontal), and lambdoid (parietal-supraoccipital) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a standard anatomical definition of human skull sutures, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In zebrafish, most if not all sutures remain patent throughout life.
source: In some continuously growing vertebrates (e.g. zebrafish), most if not all sutures remain patent throughout life (Cubbage and Mabee, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cubbage and Mabee, 1996.

claim: In groups of archosaurs and monotreme, marsupial, and placental mammals, sutures can be transient structures.
source: In other tetrapods, including groups of archosaurs (Bailleul et al., 2016) and monotreme, marsupial, and placental mammals (Rager et al., 2014), sutures can be transient structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bailleul et al., 2016 and Rager et al., 2014.

claim: Most sutures begin to close shortly after puberty in humans.
source: For example, most sutures begin to close shortly after puberty in humans.
evidence: This is a well-known fact about human skull development.

claim: The general pattern of the major sutures is largely conserved across vertebrates.
source: Nonetheless, the general pattern of the major sutures is largely conserved across vertebrates, although gain or loss of specific sutures has been linked with evolutionary changes in skull morphology.
evidence: This is a general observation about vertebrate skull evolution.

claim: Gain or loss of specific sutures has been linked with evolutionary changes in skull morphology.
source: Nonetheless, the general pattern of the major sutures is largely conserved across vertebrates, although gain or loss of specific sutures has been linked with evolutionary changes in skull morphology.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and evolutionary biology.

claim: Craniosynostosis occurs in approximately one in 2500 live births.
source: The premature loss of sutures during human fetal life is seen in craniosynostosis, a birth defect that occurs in approximately one in 2500 live births (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Twigg and Wilkie, 2015.

claim: Without surgical intervention, altered skull growth in craniosynostosis may have an adverse effect on brain development.
source: Without surgical intervention, altered skull growth may have an adverse effect on brain development.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about the consequences of craniosynostosis.

claim: Re-fusion of the separated bones in craniosynostosis often necessitates additional surgeries.
source: Unfortunately, re-fusion of the separated bones often necessitates additional surgeries.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about the treatment of craniosynostosis.

claim: Many syndromic synostoses are highly specific to particular sutures.
source: Many of these syndromic synostoses are highly specific to particular sutures, suggesting unique developmental sensitivities of each type of suture.
evidence: This is an observation from clinical genetics and developmental biology.

claim: The sagittal suture is most often affected in non-syndromic craniosynostosis.
source: Whereas the sagittal is most often affected in non-syndromic craniosynostosis, the coronal is most frequently perturbed in syndromic cases.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about craniosynostosis patterns.

claim: The coronal suture is most frequently perturbed in syndromic craniosynostosis.
source: Whereas the sagittal is most often affected in non-syndromic craniosynostosis, the coronal is most frequently perturbed in syndromic cases.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about craniosynostosis patterns.

claim: Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is the most common form of syndromic coronal synostosis.
source: The most common form of syndromic coronal synostosis is Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (Figure 1A), which is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in TWIST1 or TCF12 (el Ghouzzi et al., 1997; Howard et al., 1997; Sharma et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to el Ghouzzi et al., 1997; Howard et al., 1997; Sharma et al., 2013, and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in TWIST1 or TCF12.
source: The most common form of syndromic coronal synostosis is Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (Figure 1A), which is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in TWIST1 or TCF12 (el Ghouzzi et al., 1997; Howard et al., 1997; Sharma et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to el Ghouzzi et al., 1997; Howard et al., 1997; Sharma et al., 2013.

claim: Mouse and zebrafish models for Saethre-Chotzen syndrome reveal deep conservation of the genetic programs underlying coronal suture development.
source: Research resulting from the recent development of both mouse and zebrafish models for Saethre-Chotzen syndrome reveals deep conservation of the genetic programs underlying coronal suture development, despite dramatic shifts in the embryonic origins of the bones that abut this suture (Sharma et al., 2013; Teng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sharma et al., 2013 and Teng et al., 2018.

claim: The mouse and zebrafish lineages split from the human lineage circa 62 and 420 million years ago, respectively.
source: The mouse and zebrafish models belong to lineages that split from the human lineage circa 62 and 420 million years ago, respectively (Benton et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Benton et al., 2015.

claim: The pattern of the skull vault has diverged substantially from the common ancestors of rodents and primates, and from the two major lineages of bony fishes.
source: During these long time-intervals, the pattern of the skull vault has diverged substantially from the common ancestors of rodents and primates on one side, and from the two major lineages of bony fishes, the sarcopterygians (lobe-finned fish) and the actinopterygians (ray-finned fish).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and paleontology.

claim: Taxonomic identification and phylogenetic reconstructions based on the vertebrate fossil record rest in large part on deciphering the transformation of the skull roof pattern.
source: Taxonomic identification and phylogenetic reconstructions based on the vertebrate fossil record rest in large part on deciphering the transformation of the skull roof pattern, which is often well preserved in fossils.
evidence: This is a statement about paleontological methodology.

claim: Recognition of homologies in the skull is based solely on the topological arrangement of the bones.
source: Recognition of homologies is, however, based solely on the topological arrangement of the bones; developmental and genetic data can rarely be used as evidence (Wagner, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wagner, 2007.

claim: Names of the 'fish' bones were originally based on mammalian terminology, itself derived from human terminology.
source: Names of the 'fish' bones were originally based on mammalian terminology, itself derived from human terminology (Hanken and Hall, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hanken and Hall, 1993.

claim: Frontal bones are a newly appearing feature of tetrapodomorphs.
source: Based on this criterion, Schultze (2008a), summing up almost a century of discussion, argued that frontal bones are a newly appearing feature of tetrapodomorphs (Schultze, 2008a), a lineage of sarcopterygians including modern tetrapods and their ancestral relatives but distinct from the lungfishes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schultze, 2008a.

claim: The pineal foramen is located in the roof of the diencephalon.
source: The pineal foramen is one such landmark based on its position in the roof of the diencephalon, thus allowing placement of particular bones relative to the brain.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact about the pineal foramen.

claim: The pineal foramen was ancestrally present in osteichthyans.
source: The pineal foramen was ancestrally present in osteichthyans, but was lost independently along the actinopterygian lineage, and several times within the sarcopterygian clade (e.g. along coelacanth, lungfish, bird, and mammalian lineages; see Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and paleontology, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The pineal organ arises from an evagination of the third ventricle of the diencephalon, just posterior to the telencephalon.
source: Developmentally, the pineal organ arises from an evagination of the third ventricle of the diencephalon, just posterior to the telencephalon.
evidence: This is a developmental biology fact about the pineal organ.

claim: The telencephalon-diencephalon boundary appears to coincide with the boundary of neural crest and mesoderm germ layer contribution to the skull bones in rodents.
source: As the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary appears to coincide with the boundary of neural crest and mesoderm germ layer contribution to the skull bones in rodents (Papp et al., 2015) and zebrafish (Blümel et al., 2019), the pineal foramen, being posterior to this boundary, would be a landmark for the mesoderm-derived bone (i.e. the parietal in mammals).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Papp et al., 2015 and Blümel et al., 2019.

claim: The telencephalon-diencephalon boundary appears to coincide with the boundary of neural crest and mesoderm germ layer contribution to the skull bones in zebrafish.
source: As the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary appears to coincide with the boundary of neural crest and mesoderm germ layer contribution to the skull bones in rodents (Papp et al., 2015) and zebrafish (Blümel et al., 2019), the pineal foramen, being posterior to this boundary, would be a landmark for the mesoderm-derived bone (i.e. the parietal in mammals).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Papp et al., 2015 and Blümel et al., 2019.

claim: In Guiyu, the pineal foramen opens on the sagittal suture between the parietals and has no contact with the postrostral bones.
source: The pineal foramen opens on the sagittal suture between the parietals and has no contact with the postrostral bones; this position of the pineal foramen is a major reason we consider these bones to be parietals and not frontals (Qiao and Zhu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qiao and Zhu, 2010.

claim: In Raynerius, the pineal foramen opens between a pair of bones that would be termed parietals.
source: In the basal actinopterygian Raynerius, the pineal foramen also opens between a pair of bones that we would hence term parietals, despite these being previously referred to as 'frontals' based on conventional actinopterygian terminology (Giles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Giles et al., 2015.

claim: In basal Devonian actinopterygians, the parietals suture medially to a postrostral bone at their anterior ends, with this postrostral containing the pineal foramen.
source: In basal Devonian actinopterygians, such as Meemannia, Dialipina (also regarded as a stem osteichthyan in some recent phylogenies Clement et al., 2018), and Cheirolepis, the parietals suture medially to a postrostral bone at their anterior ends, with this postrostral containing the pineal foramen (called the pineal plate) (Figure 2) (Arratia and Cloutier, 1996; Mickle, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arratia and Cloutier, 1996; Mickle, 2015, and reference to Figure 2.

claim: In teleosteans, the rostral bones are fused to the ethmoid endoskeleton, and the dermal component is no longer distinguishable in the more derived teleosts.
source: In teleosteans (the largest class of actinopterygians), the rostral bones are fused to the ethmoid endoskeleton, and the dermal component is no longer distinguishable in the more derived teleosts (Patterson, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patterson, 1975.

claim: In zebrafish, the bones of the skull roof located anterior to the parietals are the nasals.
source: In these fishes, such as the zebrafish, the bones of the skull roof located anterior to the parietals (previously referred to as frontals) are the nasals (see Figures 1 and 2 for revised terminology).
evidence: This is a statement about zebrafish skull anatomy, with reference to Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In zebrafish, the nasals may touch the parietals or rest on them, but they do not attach to them through a fibrous suture.
source: The nasals may touch the parietals or rest on them, but they do not attach to them through a fibrous suture.
evidence: This is an observation about zebrafish skull anatomy.

claim: In gars, the snout is elongated and the parietal bone has shifted anteriorly and does not cover the anterior part of the brain.
source: For instance, in gars the skull pattern is highly derived. In these fishes, the snout is elongated and the parietal bone has shifted anteriorly and does not cover the anterior part of the brain (Grande, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grande, 2010.

claim: The 'frontal' of actinopterygians may be generally homologous to the 'parietal' of sarcopterygians.
source: It is thus reasonable to assume that the 'frontal' of actinoptergyians may be generally homologous to the 'parietal' of sarcopterygians, though this remains open to debate.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparative anatomy.

claim: In basal forms of Dipnomorpha, paired parietals are connected anteriorly to a mosaic of postrostrals.
source: In the sarcopterygian lineage, containing the mouse and the human, basal forms of Dipnomorpha (lungfishes and their relatives such as Powichthys from the Devonian of Canada and Spitsbergen) have paired parietals connected anteriorly to a mosaic of postrostrals.
evidence: This is a statement about fossil anatomy.

claim: In Powichthys, the pineal foramen is located in the middle of the postrostrals.
source: In these fishes, the pineal foramen is located in the middle of the postrostrals, thus placing the parietals even further posterior than in the stem osteichthyan Guiyu (Clement and Janvier, 2004) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clement and Janvier, 2004, and reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Eusthenopteron, the pineal foramen opens between the parietals, similar to the stem osteichthyan condition.
source: In the basal tetrapodomorph Eusthenopteron, from the Devonian of Canada, bones anterior to the parietals are a medial postrostral and two lateral series of nasals. The pineal foramen opens between the parietals, similar to the stem osteichthyan condition (Westoll, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Westoll, 1937.

claim: A trend in basal tetrapods is the elongation of the snout, which is associated with the emergence of a pair of bones corresponding to what have traditionally been called 'frontals' in the mammalian literature.
source: A trend in basal tetrapods is the elongation of the snout, which is associated with the emergence of a pair of bones corresponding to what have traditionally been called 'frontals' in the mammalian literature (Schultze, 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schultze, 2008a.

claim: The frontal appears in the Devonian at some stage along the stem-tetrapod lineage, between the Eusthenopteron and the Panderichthys clades.
source: The frontal appears in the Devonian at some stage along the stem-tetrapod lineage, between the Eusthenopteron and the Panderichthys clades (Clack, 2012) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clack, 2012, and reference to Figure 2.

claim: In basal tetrapodomorphs possessing a frontal, the suture between this bone and the parietal, which corresponds to the coronal suture, is situated at the level of the orbit.
source: In basal tetrapodomorphs possessing a frontal (e.g. Panderichthys), the suture between this bone and the parietal, which corresponds to the coronal suture, is situated at the level of the orbit.
evidence: This is an observation about fossil anatomy.

claim: The coronal suture shifted posteriorly relative to the orbits in later tetrapods.
source: The coronal suture then shifted posteriorly relative to the orbits in later tetrapods (Schultze and Arsenault, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schultze and Arsenault, 1985.

claim: In tetrapodomorphs in which the pineal foramen is still visible, it is commonly located between what are called the parietal bones.
source: Nonetheless, in tetrapodomorphs in which the pineal foramen is still visible, it is commonly located between what are called the parietal bones, despite shifts in their relation to the orbits along the tetrapod lineage.
evidence: This is an observation about fossil anatomy.

claim: The parietal of sarcopterygians would be homologous to the 'frontal' of stem osteichthyans and actinopterygians.
source: In summary, at least in reference to the pineal foramen, the parietal of sarcopterygians would be homologous to the 'frontal' of stem osteichthyans and actinopterygians, thus justifying renaming it a 'parietal' in the latter based on evolutionary continuity (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and evolutionary continuity, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The tetrapod frontal corresponds either to a neoformation or to the division of the parietal bone of basal osteichthyans into parietal and frontal bones.
source: In tetrapodomorphs, a new bone, the true frontal, intercalates between the parietal and the postrostral(s). The new frontal bone corresponds either to a neoformation or to the division of the parietal bone of basal osteichthyans into parietal and frontal bones.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the evolutionary origin of the frontal bone.

claim: The tetrapod frontal corresponds to the part of the ancestral parietal with a neural crest origin, with the parietal having exclusively a mesodermal origin.
source: In the latter case, we hypothesize that the tetrapod frontal corresponds to the part of the ancestral parietal with a neural crest origin, with the parietal having exclusively a mesodermal origin (with exceptions, such as the African clawed frog, see below).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the germ layer origins of the frontal and parietal bones.

claim: In the mouse, the posterior end of the parietal sutures with the interparietal bone.
source: In the mouse, the posterior end of the parietal sutures with the interparietal bone (itself a fusion of medial postparietal and lateral tabular bones Koyabu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koyabu et al., 2012.

claim: The actinopterygian 'parietal' is homologous to the mammalian 'postparietal'.
source: If we interpret the actinopterygian 'frontal' as the equivalent of the mammalian 'parietal', then evolutionary continuity would dictate that what is called the 'parietal' in actinopterygians is homologous to the mammalian 'postparietal' (incorporation of the tabulars into the interparietal occurred later along the amniote lineage).
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary continuity.

claim: The actinopterygian coronal suture being at a parietal-postparietal interface would be homologous to the mammalian lambdoid suture.
source: As the parietal-interparietal joint of mouse is the lambdoid suture, the actinopterygian coronal suture being at a parietal-postparietal interface would therefore be homologous to the mammalian lambdoid suture.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary continuity and comparative anatomy.

claim: Basal sarcopterygians, and possibly stem osteichthyans, had a braincase composed of two bones articulated through an intracranial joint.
source: Basal sarcopterygians, and possibly stem osteichthyans (Lu et al., 2017), had a braincase composed of two bones articulated through an intracranial joint – a hinge with considerable flexibility compared to standard sutures.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2017.

claim: The only living vertebrate with an intracranial joint is the coelacanth Latimeria.
source: The only living vertebrate with an intracranial joint is the coelacanth Latimeria.
evidence: This is a well-known fact about coelacanth anatomy.

claim: In Latimeria, there are two pairs of parietals roofing the anterior part of the braincase.
source: In Latimeria, as in most extinct coelacanths, there are two pairs of parietals roofing the anterior part of the braincase (Forey, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Forey, 1998.

claim: In coelacanth fetuses, the pineal complex and the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary are located at the level of the anterior parietal.
source: Recent analysis of coelacanth fetuses (Dutel et al., 2019) has revealed that the pineal complex, not visible on the surface of the brain (Hafeez and Merhige, 1977), and the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary are located at the level of the anterior parietal, according to Forey (1998), suggesting homology with the parietal of other osteichthyans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dutel et al., 2019; Hafeez and Merhige, 1977; Forey, 1998.

claim: Intercalation of a new bone (the posterior parietal) along the coelacanth lineage shifted the intracranial joint from a 'parietal'-'postparietal' interface to a 'posterior parietal'-'postparietal' interface.
source: We therefore suggest that intercalation of a new bone (the posterior parietal) along the coelacanth lineage shifted the intracranial joint from a 'parietal'-'postparietal' interface (as with the zebrafish 'coronal' and mouse 'lambdoid' suture) to a 'posterior parietal'-'postparietal' interface.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about coelacanth skull evolution.

claim: Closure of the intracranial joint and suturing of the parietal with the postparietal occurred several times in the evolutionary history of osteichthyans.
source: Closure of the intracranial joint and suturing of the parietal with the postparietal occurred several times in the evolutionary history of osteichthyans, possibly at the base of the actinopterygian lineage, and certainly along the lungfish and tetrapodomorph lineages (Lu et al., 2017) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Acquisition of the mammalian lambdoid and zebrafish coronal sutures would reflect convergent evolution.
source: As a consequence, acquisition of the mammalian lambdoid and zebrafish coronal sutures would reflect convergent evolution, although their positioning at a common parietal-postparietal interface could still reflect the common developmental processes discussed below.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary relationship between the mammalian lambdoid and zebrafish coronal sutures.

claim: The parietal is a conserved structure across taxa.
source: We can infer from fossil data that the parietal is a conserved structure across taxa, while the true frontal is a novel bone evolved in the tetrapodomorph lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on paleontological data.

claim: The true frontal is a novel bone evolved in the tetrapodomorph lineage.
source: We can infer from fossil data that the parietal is a conserved structure across taxa, while the true frontal is a novel bone evolved in the tetrapodomorph lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on paleontological data.

claim: The tetrapod coronal suture, as defined by a frontal-parietal interface, would be non-existent in actinopterygians including the zebrafish.
source: Thus, the tetrapod coronal suture, as defined by a frontal-parietal interface, would be non-existent in actinopterygians including the zebrafish.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and evolutionary continuity.

claim: The 'coronal suture' of actinopterygians would be analogous to the lambdoid suture of mouse.
source: Instead, the 'coronal suture' of these species would be analogous to the lambdoid suture of mouse.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and evolutionary continuity.

claim: In mouse, use of a Wnt1-Cre allele shows that the coronal suture forms at a clear boundary between the neural crest-derived frontal and mesoderm-derived parietal bones.
source: In mouse, use of a Wnt1-Cre allele to indelibly mark neural crest derivatives (Jiang et al., 2002), and a Mesp1-Cre allele to mark mesodermal derivatives (Yoshida et al., 2008), shows that the coronal suture forms at a clear boundary between the neural crest-derived frontal and mesoderm-derived parietal bones; the fibrous tissue of the suture itself is largely mesoderm-derived (Merrill et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2008; Merrill et al., 2006.

claim: In mouse, the fibrous tissue of the coronal suture is largely mesoderm-derived.
source: In mouse, use of a Wnt1-Cre allele to indelibly mark neural crest derivatives (Jiang et al., 2002), and a Mesp1-Cre allele to mark mesodermal derivatives (Yoshida et al., 2008), shows that the coronal suture forms at a clear boundary between the neural crest-derived frontal and mesoderm-derived parietal bones; the fibrous tissue of the suture itself is largely mesoderm-derived (Merrill et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Merrill et al., 2006.

claim: In chick, Evans and Noden concluded that the frontal bone is of dual origin.
source: In 2006, Evans and Noden performed more precise labeling of both neural crest and mesoderm cells with retroviral injections and concluded that the frontal bone is of dual origin (Evans and Noden, 2006), with the 'coronal suture' at the border of the mesoderm portion of the frontal and the mesoderm-derived parietal bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Evans and Noden, 2006.

claim: In chick, the 'coronal suture' is at the border of the mesoderm portion of the frontal and the mesoderm-derived parietal bone.
source: In 2006, Evans and Noden performed more precise labeling of both neural crest and mesoderm cells with retroviral injections and concluded that the frontal bone is of dual origin (Evans and Noden, 2006), with the 'coronal suture' at the border of the mesoderm portion of the frontal and the mesoderm-derived parietal bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Evans and Noden, 2006.

claim: Lineage tracing of neural crest derivatives in zebrafish revealed a dual origin of the 'frontal' bone.
source: Similar to chick, lineage tracing of neural crest derivatives in zebrafish with a Sox10-Cre allele revealed a dual origin of the 'frontal' bone (the homolog of the mammalian parietal based on paleontological evidence), with the 'coronal suture' sitting at a mesoderm-mesoderm boundary (Kague et al., 2012; Mongera et al., 2013) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kague et al., 2012; Mongera et al., 2013, and reference to Figure 3.

claim: In zebrafish, the 'coronal suture' sits at a mesoderm-mesoderm boundary.
source: Similar to chick, lineage tracing of neural crest derivatives in zebrafish with a Sox10-Cre allele revealed a dual origin of the 'frontal' bone (the homolog of the mammalian parietal based on paleontological evidence), with the 'coronal suture' sitting at a mesoderm-mesoderm boundary (Kague et al., 2012; Mongera et al., 2013) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kague et al., 2012; Mongera et al., 2013, and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Grafting of GFP-labeled neural crest or mesoderm in the Mexican axolotl revealed the 'coronal suture' to be at a neural crest-mesoderm boundary.
source: Grafting of GFP-labeled neural crest or mesoderm in the Mexican axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) revealed the 'coronal suture' to be at a neural crest-mesoderm boundary, as in mice (Maddin et al., 2016), yet in the African clawed frog (Xenopus laevis) neural crest grafts suggest that the 'coronal suture' lies at a neural crest-neural crest boundary (Piekarski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maddin et al., 2016.

claim: In the African clawed frog, neural crest grafts suggest that the 'coronal suture' lies at a neural crest-neural crest boundary.
source: Grafting of GFP-labeled neural crest or mesoderm in the Mexican axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) revealed the 'coronal suture' to be at a neural crest-mesoderm boundary, as in mice (Maddin et al., 2016), yet in the African clawed frog (Xenopus laevis) neural crest grafts suggest that the 'coronal suture' lies at a neural crest-neural crest boundary (Piekarski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Piekarski et al., 2014.

claim: The mouse and zebrafish coronal sutures are positioned at dissimilar tissue-origin boundaries.
source: In summary, lineage-tracing experiments demonstrate that the mouse and zebrafish coronal sutures are positioned at dissimilar tissue-origin boundaries, in agreement with analyses of comparative morphology and the fossil record.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on lineage tracing data and comparative anatomy.

claim: The chick coronal suture may be a modified homolog of the mouse coronal suture.
source: Notably, we propose that the chick coronal suture may be a modified homolog of the mouse coronal suture, whereas the zebrafish coronal suture is homologous to the mouse lambdoid suture.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about suture homology.

claim: The zebrafish coronal suture is homologous to the mouse lambdoid suture.
source: Notably, we propose that the chick coronal suture may be a modified homolog of the mouse coronal suture, whereas the zebrafish coronal suture is homologous to the mouse lambdoid suture.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about suture homology.

claim: Skull bones appear, disappear, and fuse frequently during evolution.
source: It also becomes apparent that skull bones appear (e.g. tetrapodomorph frontal, coelacanth posterior parietal), disappear (e.g. chicken postparietal), and fuse (e.g. chicken frontal and postorbital) frequently during evolution, complicating the assignment of suture homology across vertebrates.
evidence: This is a general observation about skull evolution.

claim: Limb buds represent deep, serial homologs of the pharyngeal arches.
source: For example, it has been proposed that limb buds represent deep, serial homologs of the pharyngeal arches (but see Rui and Molnar, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about deep homology, with a citation to Rui and Molnar, 2014.

claim: The embryonic brain is in intimate association with the overlying mesenchyme that will form the bony calvarium.
source: The embryonic brain is an attractive candidate for providing such suture-inducing signals, as it is in intimate association with the overlying mesenchyme that will form the bony calvarium that protects it.
evidence: This is a statement about embryonic anatomy.

claim: The embryonic brain is subdivided by signaling centers, such as at the telencephalon-diencephalon, forebrain-midbrain, and midbrain-hindbrain boundaries.
source: In addition, the embryonic brain is subdivided by signaling centers, such as at the telencephalon-diencephalon, forebrain-midbrain, and midbrain-hindbrain boundaries, and these are rich in signaling molecules known to be important in controlling osteogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about embryonic brain development.

claim: Excision of the midbrain and hindbrain in chicken resulted in loss of the parietal bone.
source: In the late 1960s, Schowing examined the role of the chicken brain in skull bone development, finding, for example, that excision of the midbrain and hindbrain resulted in loss of the parietal bone (Schowing, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schowing, 1968.

claim: The frontal bone is invariably found above the forebrain in reptiles and birds.
source: More recently, Fabbri et al. evaluated skull morphology across numerous reptiles and birds and noted that the frontal bone is invariably found above the forebrain, and the parietal bone above the midbrain (Fabbri et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fabbri et al., 2017.

claim: The parietal bone is invariably found above the midbrain in reptiles and birds.
source: More recently, Fabbri et al. evaluated skull morphology across numerous reptiles and birds and noted that the frontal bone is invariably found above the forebrain, and the parietal bone above the midbrain (Fabbri et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fabbri et al., 2017.

claim: In a variety of mammals, the coronal suture aligns with the middle of the forebrain.
source: In a variety of mammals, the coronal suture aligns with the middle of the forebrain (Blümel et al., 2019), roughly where the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary and pineal gland develop (Sood, 1980), and molecular analysis in mouse supports alignment of the coronal suture with the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary (Deckelbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blümel et al., 2019; Sood, 1980; Deckelbaum et al., 2012.

claim: The lambdoid suture is located just anterior to the cerebellum in mouse.
source: The lambdoid suture, which separates the parietal and interparietal bones of mouse, is located just anterior to the cerebellum, a structure derived from the midbrain-hindbrain isthmus (Papp et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Papp et al., 2015.

claim: Signals from the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary specify the mammalian, and possibly the avian, coronal suture in part by keeping the frontal and parietal bone anlagen separate.
source: We suggest a model in which signals from the telencephalon-diencephalon boundary (also known as the zona limitans intrathalamica, or ZLI) specify the mammalian, and possibly the avian, coronal suture in part by keeping the frontal and parietal bone anlagen separate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on anatomical correlations, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The mid-hindbrain boundary would perform an analogous role in specifying the murine lambdoid suture.
source: More posteriorly, the mid-hindbrain boundary (MHB) would perform an analogous role in specifying the murine lambdoid suture, and by implication the zebrafish coronal suture if we consider it homologous to the murine lambdoid suture (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on anatomical correlations, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Conditional deletion of one copy of Twist1 in the mesoderm or neural crest of mouse can shift the location of the coronal suture.
source: Consistent with this, conditional deletion of one copy of Twist1 in the mesoderm or neural crest of mouse can shift the location of the coronal suture due to tissue-autonomous acceleration of parietal or frontal bone growth, respectively (Teng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Teng et al., 2018.

claim: Fgf8 and Fgf17 are present at or near the ZLI and MHB.
source: Fgf8 and Fgf17 are present at or near the ZLI and MHB (Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012; Xu et al., 1999), and Fgf8 is required for development of the forebrain-midbrain (Scholpp et al., 2003) and midbrain-hindbrain (Lee et al., 1997) boundaries.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012; Xu et al., 1999; Scholpp et al., 2003; Lee et al., 1997.

claim: Fgf8 is required for development of the forebrain-midbrain boundary.
source: Fgf8 and Fgf17 are present at or near the ZLI and MHB (Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012; Xu et al., 1999), and Fgf8 is required for development of the forebrain-midbrain (Scholpp et al., 2003) and midbrain-hindbrain (Lee et al., 1997) boundaries.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scholpp et al., 2003.

claim: Fgf8 is required for development of the midbrain-hindbrain boundary.
source: Fgf8 and Fgf17 are present at or near the ZLI and MHB (Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012; Xu et al., 1999), and Fgf8 is required for development of the forebrain-midbrain (Scholpp et al., 2003) and midbrain-hindbrain (Lee et al., 1997) boundaries.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 1997.

claim: Loss of the coronal suture is seen in several human syndromes caused by mutations in Fgf receptors: Pfeiffer (FGFR1), Apert (FGFR2), Beare-Stevenson (FGFR2), Crouzon (FGFR2), and Muenke (FGFR3).
source: Loss of the coronal suture is seen in several human syndromes caused by mutations in Fgf receptors: Pfeiffer (FGFR1), Apert (FGFR2), Beare-Stevenson (FGFR2), Crouzon (FGFR2), and Muenke (FGFR3) (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Twigg and Wilkie, 2015.

claim: Fgf8 has been shown to induce En2 expression.
source: At similar stages, En1 is expressed in supraorbital ridge mesenchyme near the ZLI prior to calvarial bone development (Figure 4B), and lineage tracing of these En1+ cells revealed contribution to the coronal suture mesenchyme (Deckelbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 1997 (mentioned earlier in the text).

claim: En1 is expressed in supraorbital ridge mesenchyme near the ZLI prior to calvarial bone development.
source: At similar stages, En1 is expressed in supraorbital ridge mesenchyme near the ZLI prior to calvarial bone development (Figure 4B), and lineage tracing of these En1+ cells revealed contribution to the coronal suture mesenchyme (Deckelbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deckelbaum et al., 2012, and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Lineage tracing of En1+ cells revealed contribution to the coronal suture mesenchyme.
source: At similar stages, En1 is expressed in supraorbital ridge mesenchyme near the ZLI prior to calvarial bone development (Figure 4B), and lineage tracing of these En1+ cells revealed contribution to the coronal suture mesenchyme (Deckelbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deckelbaum et al., 2012.

claim: Wnt2b, Wnt5a, and Wnt8b are expressed at or bordering the ZLI.
source: Wnt signaling has also been implicated in suture development, with Wnt2b, Wnt5a, and Wnt8b expressed at or bordering the ZLI (Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012), Wnt1 at the MHB, and Wnt3a at both the ZLI and MHB (Dorsky et al., 1998; Quinlan et al., 2009) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012, and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Wnt1 is expressed at the MHB.
source: Wnt signaling has also been implicated in suture development, with Wnt2b, Wnt5a, and Wnt8b expressed at or bordering the ZLI (Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012), Wnt1 at the MHB, and Wnt3a at both the ZLI and MHB (Dorsky et al., 1998; Quinlan et al., 2009) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dorsky et al., 1998; Quinlan et al., 2009, and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Wnt3a is expressed at both the ZLI and MHB.
source: Wnt signaling has also been implicated in suture development, with Wnt2b, Wnt5a, and Wnt8b expressed at or bordering the ZLI (Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012), Wnt1 at the MHB, and Wnt3a at both the ZLI and MHB (Dorsky et al., 1998; Quinlan et al., 2009) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dorsky et al., 1998; Quinlan et al., 2009, and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The negative Wnt regulator Axin2 is prominently expressed at the coronal suture of mice.
source: The negative Wnt regulator Axin2 is also prominently expressed at the coronal suture of mice (Yu et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2005.

claim: Mutations in mouse Axin2 have been reported to cause craniosynostosis.
source: Mutations in mouse Axin2 (Behr et al., 2013) and human AXIN2 (Yilmaz et al., 2018) have been reported to cause craniosynostosis, although the metopic and sagittal sutures and not the coronal are most commonly affected by mutations in these orthologous genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Behr et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations in human AXIN2 have been reported to cause craniosynostosis.
source: Mutations in mouse Axin2 (Behr et al., 2013) and human AXIN2 (Yilmaz et al., 2018) have been reported to cause craniosynostosis, although the metopic and sagittal sutures and not the coronal are most commonly affected by mutations in these orthologous genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yilmaz et al., 2018.

claim: Shh is expressed at the ZLI but not the MHB.
source: Of note, Shh is expressed at the ZLI but not the MHB (Jeong et al., 2011) (Figure 4B), suggesting that differential Hh activity might help explain sensitivities of the coronal versus lambdoid suture to genetic perturbations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeong et al., 2011, and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Signals from the brain and olfactory epithelium pattern the nasal cartilage that in turn helps shape facial intramembranous bones.
source: Intriguingly, a role for brain signaling in patterning the skull may not be limited to the calvarium, as a recent report suggests that signals from the brain and olfactory epithelium pattern the nasal cartilage that in turn helps shape facial intramembranous bones (Kaucka et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kaucka et al., 2018.

claim: The closure of sutures at puberty in humans coincides with endochondral ossification between the fusing bones.
source: In humans, the closure of sutures at puberty coincides with endochondral ossification, i.e. cartilage-templated bone formation, between the fusing bones (Pritchard et al., 1956).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pritchard et al., 1956.

claim: Normal closure of the mouse posterior frontal suture is accompanied by a cartilage intermediate.
source: Similarly, normal closure of the mouse posterior frontal suture is accompanied by a cartilage intermediate (Sahar et al., 2005), and loss of the coronal suture in mice with gain-of-function Pdgfra signaling is accompanied by ectopic cartilage between the frontal and parietal bones (He and Soriano, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sahar et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of the coronal suture in mice with gain-of-function Pdgfra signaling is accompanied by ectopic cartilage between the frontal and parietal bones.
source: Similarly, normal closure of the mouse posterior frontal suture is accompanied by a cartilage intermediate (Sahar et al., 2005), and loss of the coronal suture in mice with gain-of-function Pdgfra signaling is accompanied by ectopic cartilage between the frontal and parietal bones (He and Soriano, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He and Soriano, 2017.

claim: Zebrafish have a prominent cartilage rod, termed the epiphyseal bar, which runs across the entire roof of the skull at the boundary of neural crest- and mesoderm-derived mesenchyme.
source: Whereas zebrafish do not develop a suture at this location, there is a prominent cartilage rod, termed the epiphyseal bar, which runs across the entire roof of the skull at the boundary of neural crest- and mesoderm-derived mesenchyme (Kague et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kague et al., 2016.

claim: At the neural crest-mesoderm boundary in mouse, only short cartilage bars, termed the tectum transversum, are seen at both the left and right supraorbital ridges.
source: In contrast, at the neural crest-mesoderm boundary in mouse, only short cartilage bars, termed the tectum transversum, are seen at both the left and right supraorbital ridges; these do not connect across the skull roof (Percival and Richtsmeier, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Percival and Richtsmeier, 2017.

claim: The epiphyseal bar is maintained through adulthood in zebrafish.
source: Further, the epiphyseal bar is maintained through adulthood in zebrafish, yet the tectum transversum is largely resorbed by adult stages in mouse.
evidence: This is an observation about zebrafish anatomy.

claim: The tectum transversum is largely resorbed by adult stages in mouse.
source: Further, the epiphyseal bar is maintained through adulthood in zebrafish, yet the tectum transversum is largely resorbed by adult stages in mouse.
evidence: This is an observation about mouse anatomy.

claim: The full-length cartilage bar in zebrafish prevents the formation of a suture in the analogous position to where the mouse coronal suture forms.
source: One possibility is that the full-length cartilage bar in zebrafish prevents the formation of a suture in the analogous position to where the mouse coronal suture forms.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the role of the epiphyseal bar.

claim: The Mesozoic teleost fish Leptolepis lacks a suture where the epiphyseal bar cartilage has left a groove in the skull.
source: Such a model is supported by analysis of one of the earliest known teleost fishes, the Mesozoic Leptolepis, which similarly lacks a suture where the epiphyseal bar cartilage has left a groove in the skull (Patterson, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patterson, 1975.

claim: In postnatal mice, ablation of the Gli1+ sutural stem cells that fuel continued bone growth results in a complete loss of all sutures.
source: In postnatal mice, ablation of the Gli1+ sutural stem cells that fuel continued bone growth results in a complete loss of all sutures (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: An earlier embryonic defect in frontal and parietal bone growth may be the cause of the later loss of the coronal suture in mice and zebrafish harboring mutations in homologs of TWIST1 and TCF12.
source: In contrast, an earlier embryonic defect in frontal and parietal bone growth may be the cause of the later loss of the coronal suture in mice and zebrafish harboring mutations in homologs of TWIST1 and TCF12 (Teng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Teng et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of the coronal suture in Fuz mutant mice is reflected by a failure to form separate frontal and parietal bone ossification centers.
source: Finally, loss of the coronal suture in Fuz mutant mice is reflected by a failure to form separate frontal and parietal bone ossification centers (Tabler et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tabler et al., 2016.

claim: Breakdown of the boundary between the fibrous suture and the adjacent osteogenic mesenchyme is associated with suture loss.
source: Other studies have shown that breakdown of the boundary between the fibrous suture and the adjacent osteogenic mesenchyme is associated with suture loss (Merrill et al., 2006; Ting et al., 2009; Yen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Merrill et al., 2006; Ting et al., 2009; Yen et al., 2010.

claim: Eph-ephrin signaling has well known roles in establishing tissue boundaries in a number of organs.
source: For example, Eph-ephrin signaling has well known roles in establishing tissue boundaries in a number of organs (Cayuso et al., 2015), and mutations in EFNB1 result in coronal synostosis in humans (Twigg et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cayuso et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations in EFNB1 result in coronal synostosis in humans.
source: For example, Eph-ephrin signaling has well known roles in establishing tissue boundaries in a number of organs (Cayuso et al., 2015), and mutations in EFNB1 result in coronal synostosis in humans (Twigg et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Twigg et al., 2004.

claim: In mouse, the ligands ephrin-A2 and ephrin-A4 are expressed in cells overlying the coronal suture region and prospective frontal bone, in what is termed the ectocranial layer.
source: In mouse, the ligands ephrin-A2 and ephrin-A4 are expressed in cells overlying the coronal suture region and prospective frontal bone, in what is termed the ectocranial layer, and the receptor EphA4 is expressed in a complementary pattern within the frontal bone and coronal suture (Merrill et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Merrill et al., 2006.

claim: The receptor EphA4 is expressed in a complementary pattern within the frontal bone and coronal suture in mouse.
source: In mouse, the ligands ephrin-A2 and ephrin-A4 are expressed in cells overlying the coronal suture region and prospective frontal bone, in what is termed the ectocranial layer, and the receptor EphA4 is expressed in a complementary pattern within the frontal bone and coronal suture (Merrill et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Merrill et al., 2006.

claim: In Epha4 mutant mice, inappropriate cell mixing was observed across the neural crest-mesoderm boundary where the coronal suture forms.
source: In Epha4 mutant mice, inappropriate cell mixing was observed across the neural crest-mesoderm boundary where the coronal suture forms (Ting et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ting et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations in homologs of the Saethre-Chotzen genes TWIST1 and TCF12 in mouse and zebrafish result in similarly specific loss of the coronal suture.
source: Unexpectedly, mutations in homologs of the Saethre-Chotzen genes TWIST1 and TCF12 in mouse and zebrafish result in similarly specific loss of the coronal suture, despite the zebrafish coronal suture likely being homologous to the mouse lambdoid suture (Teng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Teng et al., 2018.

claim: Only homozygous loss of both twist1b and tcf12 disrupts the zebrafish 'coronal'.
source: While the coronal but not lambdoid suture is affected in humans and mouse models of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, in which TWIST1 and TCF12 mutations are heterozygous, only homozygous loss of both twist1b and tcf12 disrupts the zebrafish 'coronal' (i.e. lambdoid homolog), potentially consistent with greater sensitivity of the coronal than lambdoid to TWIST1/TCF12 disruption.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Expression of Shh and Ptc has been reported to be high in the metopic and sagittal but low in the coronal suture.
source: For example, expression of Shh and Ptc has been reported to be high in the metopic and sagittal but low in the coronal suture (Kim et al., 1998), which could underlie differential sensitivities of the coronal suture to genetic changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 1998.

claim: The adult human skull is composed of 22 bones.
source: The adult human skull is composed of 22 bones, versus the 74 bones of the adult zebrafish skull, suggesting wide divergence of both species from their common ancestor circa 420 million years ago (Cubbage and Mabee, 1996; Hanken and Hall, 1993).
evidence: This is a well-known anatomical fact.

claim: The adult zebrafish skull is composed of 74 bones.
source: The adult human skull is composed of 22 bones, versus the 74 bones of the adult zebrafish skull, suggesting wide divergence of both species from their common ancestor circa 420 million years ago (Cubbage and Mabee, 1996; Hanken and Hall, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cubbage and Mabee, 1996; Hanken and Hall, 1993.

claim: The mammalian interparietals are seamless fusions of medial neural crest-derived postparietal and lateral mesoderm-derived tabular bones.
source: Lineage tracing in mouse shows that the interparietals are seamless fusions of medial neural crest-derived postparietal (Jiang et al., 2002) and lateral mesoderm-derived tabular bones (Yoshida et al., 2008), in much the same way that the chicken frontal and mammalian stapes are seamless fusions of neural crest- and mesoderm-derived bone (Thompson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2012.

claim: Bird embryos transiently display separate ossification centers corresponding to frontals and postorbitals that later fuse into a single frontal bone.
source: As discussed earlier, bird embryos transiently display separate ossification centers corresponding to frontals and postorbitals that later fuse into a single frontal bone.
evidence: This is a statement about bird development.

claim: In dinosaurian ancestors of birds, the frontals and postorbitals remain separate through adulthood.
source: In their dinosaurian ancestors, however, the frontals and postorbitals remain separate through adulthood (Smith-Paredes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith-Paredes et al., 2018.

claim: Fusion of the mesoderm-derived postorbital onto the neural crest-derived frontal may have facilitated forebrain expansion along the dinosaur-avian lineage.
source: It was further hypothesized that fusion of the mesoderm-derived postorbital onto the neural crest-derived frontal, which created a new mesoderm-mesoderm coronal suture boundary, may have facilitated forebrain expansion along the dinosaur-avian lineage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about avian evolution.

claim: Imaging of RUNX2:GFP+ pre-osteoblasts in zebrafish revealed only a single ossification center for the frontal bone.
source: In contrast, imaging of RUNX2:GFP+ pre-osteoblasts in zebrafish revealed only a single ossification center for the frontal bone, indicating that neural crest- and mesoderm-derived tissues intermix before the start of ossification (Kague et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kague et al., 2016.

claim: In zebrafish, neural crest- and mesoderm-derived tissues intermix before the start of ossification.
source: In contrast, imaging of RUNX2:GFP+ pre-osteoblasts in zebrafish revealed only a single ossification center for the frontal bone, indicating that neural crest- and mesoderm-derived tissues intermix before the start of ossification (Kague et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kague et al., 2016.
